title: Cancellations, No-Shows, and Waitlists

sections.learningObjectives:
- Handle patient cancellations and reschedule appointments accurately and professionally.
- Document no-shows objectively and perform appropriate follow-up within scope of practice.
- Maintain an effective waitlist and use it to fill open slots fairly and efficiently.
- Escalate safety concerns related to missed appointments to licensed staff promptly.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

A cancellation is when you call ahead to say, “I can’t make it” — like telling a friend in advance that you can’t come to their party.

### Question 2

When someone cancels, you say “no problem, thanks for letting us know,” and erase that appointment from the calendar so the time is free again.

### Question 3

Write down who called, when they called, and which appointment they cancelled — like leaving a note so everyone knows why a calendar spot is now empty.

### Question 4

While you have them on the phone, ask, “Would you like to pick a new day?” — like offering to rebook a dentist visit right away.

### Question 5

Tell the team “there’s an empty time now,” so someone can offer it to another patient who is waiting.

### Question 6

Be kind when someone cancels, like saying “thanks for letting us know” instead of getting annoyed.

### Question 7

If a patient asks about the rules, tell them the real office rules — don’t make something up.

### Question 8

A cancellation is like texting “I can’t come” before the event; a no-show is just not showing up with no message at all.

### Question 9

If a helper calls for someone, write down who they are and follow the office’s rules about who is allowed to make changes.

### Question 10

If one kid drops out of a game, you invite someone from the bench who wants to play — same idea with a waitlist.

### Question 11

Write down just what the office needs to know — like writing “called to cancel” instead of a person’s whole private story.

### Question 12

If someone cancels a whole set of lessons, you clear each one off the calendar — not just the first.

### Question 13

Before hanging up, repeat the new time and date so the patient can say, “Yes, that’s right!”

### Question 14

If a friend keeps cancelling, you might wonder if they need help getting there — you wouldn’t just get mad.

### Question 15

Rescheduling is like moving a playdate from Tuesday to Thursday — same plan, new day.

### Question 16

Pick a new time based on how soon the patient needs help — like putting the most urgent person first in line.

### Question 17

Ask, “Does Thursday at 2 work for you?” before writing it in ink.

### Question 18

If a test needs an empty stomach, remind them again for the new day — like re-reading the recipe before baking.

### Question 19

When you move an event, you erase the old square and write it in the new square — you don’t keep both.

### Question 20

If someone says “my chest hurts,” that’s a “tell the doctor now” moment, not a “schedule for next month” moment.

### Question 21

If the favorite teacher is full, you offer another teacher or put them on a list for openings — you don’t invent a seat.

### Question 22

If you forget to erase the old square, two people might show up for the same chair — that’s the problem.

### Question 23

Rescheduling is like moving a doctor’s visit to a new day instead of just skipping it — you still get the care you need.

### Question 24

Some appointments are like a cake that must bake for an exact time — the timing really matters.

### Question 25

Write in the chart, “moved from Monday to Thursday,” so anyone can see what changed.

### Question 26

Set an alarm for the new date, like a phone reminder, so the visit doesn’t get forgotten.

### Question 27

A video call and an in-person visit are different — you need to book the right kind and tell them how to join.

### Question 28

If the coach gets sick, the team calls everyone to pick a new practice time — you don’t leave them guessing.

### Question 29

A no-show is when someone just doesn’t come and doesn’t call — like a friend who never shows and never texts.

### Question 30

Write down the truth: “this person did not come today” — don’t make up a story about why.

### Question 31

The “missed appointment” note goes in the patient’s file, not on a sticky note at home.

### Question 32

Write only the facts — like a referee writing “player did not show up,” not “player is a bad person.”

### Question 33

Even if nothing happened, writing it down helps the team check on the person and notice if it keeps happening.

### Question 34

If a friend misses three hangouts, you check if something is wrong — you don’t ignore it.

### Question 35

Tell the team, “that patient didn’t come today,” so the right people know.

### Question 36

Keep the note locked in the chart, like keeping a secret safe — not written where everyone can see.

### Question 37

One note says “they called and cancelled,” the other says “they didn’t show up” — different notes for different things.

### Question 38

Write it down right away, like jotting down that a teammate is absent when attendance is taken.

### Question 39

If the rule is “you’re not late until 15 minutes,” then at 12 minutes you’re still okay — follow the rule.

### Question 40

Choose the button that says “did not show” — don’t mark it “done” when it wasn’t.

### Question 41

Follow-up is like checking on a friend who missed a meetup — you want to make sure they’re okay.

### Question 42

The first try is usually a phone call to see if they’re okay and to offer a new time.

### Question 43

If a test came back not-normal and the person skips their visit, that’s a “tell the doctor right away” situation.

### Question 44

Call like a caring friend: “We missed you, are you okay? Want to pick a new day?”

### Question 45

Write down “I called and left a message today,” so the team knows what was tried.

### Question 46

If they’re okay, help them pick a new day — like re-booking a missed haircut.

### Question 47

If calls don’t work, the office might send a polite letter — like mailing a note to a friend you can’t reach.

### Question 48

If someone can’t get a ride, you help them find a better time or a resource — you don’t just say “too bad.”

### Question 49

You check in soon after, not months later — like calling a friend the same day they miss lunch.

### Question 50

If they ask about a fee, tell them the real office rule — you don’t make up prices like running your own store.

### Question 51

The assistant is like the messenger — they pass the important news to the doctor, who makes the big decisions.

### Question 52

Write down every try, and if you still can’t reach them, follow the office’s plan for what to do next.

### Question 53

A waitlist is like a sign-up sheet of people who want to be called if an earlier spot opens up.

### Question 54

If the next open spot is far away and they want sooner, put their name on the “call me if something opens” list.

### Question 55

Write down their name, phone number, and when they’re free — so you can actually call them when a spot opens.

### Question 56

When someone gets a spot, cross their name off the list — like erasing a name after the person is picked.

### Question 57

Usually it’s first-come, first-served — but if someone is really sick, they may jump the line, like a patient who is hurt most being seen first.

### Question 58

When a spot opens today, you call the people on the “want a spot soon” list right away.

### Question 59

You can say “a spot opened,” but you don’t say “because Mrs. Jones cancelled” — that’s private.

### Question 60

A waitlist is a “call me if there’s room” list; overbooking is giving out more tickets than there are chairs.

### Question 61

Ask, “Can you come at 2 today?” before writing their name into that time.

### Question 62

If they don’t answer, note it and move to the next name on the list, like a coach calling the next player.

### Question 63

If they say “I don’t need a spot anymore,” take their name off the list.

### Question 64

The rule says “wait this long for an answer, then call the next person,” so the chair doesn’t stay empty.

### Question 65

An empty slot is a missed chance to help someone — filling it helps patients and keeps the office running well.

### Question 66

When a time frees up, first call the people on the “I want an earlier spot” list.

### Question 67

Check that the chair is really empty before seating someone, so two people don’t end up in the same spot.

### Question 68

Make sure the open time is the right length and the right doctor for that patient — like matching a shoe size, not just any empty spot.

### Question 69

Write the new patient into the schedule and tell the team, “someone is coming at that time now.”

### Question 70

You wouldn’t squeeze a two-hour movie into a ten-minute TV slot — find a time that actually fits.

### Question 71

Tell them exactly when and where, and set a reminder, like sending a clear invite for a last-minute meetup.

### Question 72

Counting how often chairs stay empty helps the office figure out how to fill them better — like tracking which days the bus is empty.

### Question 73

If many people miss Mondays, the office can plan extra reminders or a bigger backup list — like adding more buses on a busy route.

### Question 74

Before closing, check tomorrow’s calendar like checking your backpack the night before school.

### Question 75

If the plan changes, call the patient right away — like texting a friend when the meeting time moves.
